projects.headline: Nexys A7-100T (xc7a100tcsg324-1), Vivado 2026.1: 5 of 5 known-answer requests on one design, written in plain English, were answered from captures on the board. Every answer matched the known result, and the value read back over the serial link where a register was read back.

hero.caption: One real run replayed: the request, the plan, the build, then the capture filling in sample by sample around the trigger, and the answer read from it.

data.alt: Waveform of win_wr, addr and count from cycle -16 to 32 around the trigger: win_wr is 1 only at cycle 0, addr holds 0x80, count is 0x0003 up to cycle 0 and 0x1234 from cycle 1.
captions: Capture: the 16 cycles before the trigger come from the analyser's buffer, recorded before the trigger fired.
Cycle 0, the trigger sample: win_wr == 1 AND addr == 0x80 (win_wr = 1, addr = 0x80).
Cycle 1: count changes from 0x0003 to 0x1234, one clock after the write strobe: the register loads on the clock edge that ends it.

Request, in plain English: "First write 3 to COUNT. Then capture count, win_wr and the shell's ADDR byte when the shell writes the COUNT register (win_wr is 1 and addr is 0x80), 16 cycles before and 32 after. The write that triggers it puts 0x1234 in COUNT. Afterwards read COUNT back."

projects.one_line: Ask for a capture in words: the flow picks the signals by their RTL names, sets the trigger, builds an on-chip logic analyser, captures on the board and answers in plain words, quoting only the capture.

approvals: The owner asked for this capability, set the order (front end first) and the safety rules: board memory only, power and temperature limits, design checks never skipped. No approval was needed per run: each capture holds the board lock and programs board memory only.
gates: The plan matched its schema and the free tier's limits before any build.
The build passed every check of the normal flow, including timing and the debug hub's clock crossing.
The build ID read back over JTAG matched before arming (d2b75378).
Every number in the answer was checked against the capture.
agent.plan: Three signals resolved by RTL name to register outputs and packed into 2 of the 5 ports; the trigger on the write strobe and the address byte; a 1024-sample window, the smallest that holds the 16 cycles before and 32 after that were asked for (the answer covers only those).
agent.request: First write 3 to COUNT. Then capture count, win_wr and the shell's ADDR byte when the shell writes the COUNT register (win_wr is 1 and addr is 0x80), 16 cycles before and 32 after. The write that triggers it puts 0x1234 in COUNT. Afterwards read COUNT back.

links: the agent asks the next question

details.text: The resolver reads the RTL, not the model. Asked for 'cnt', it finds 5 different registers with that name (u_dut.u_db_clear.cnt, u_dut.u_db_down.cnt, u_dut.u_db_up.cnt, u_shell.u_rx.cnt, u_shell.u_tx.cnt) and refuses the plan with the list, instead of picking one. The model's only job is to turn a phrase into a name: 'the shell's ADDR byte' came back from the model as 'addr', which the resolver then traced to u_shell.u_core.frame[1] (pins u_shell/u_core/frame_reg[1][*]/Q); a name it cannot trace is an error with suggestions, never a guess.
details.title: When a name is ambiguous, the plan stops and asks

details.text: Every number in an answer must be a value, change, run or count of the signal its line names, inside the window asked for. 'count was 0x0003 from cycle -16 to 0, then 0x1234 from cycle 1 to 32.' passes. Changing one value, 'count was 0x0003 from cycle -16 to 0, then 0x4321 from cycle 1 to 32.', is refused: 0x4321 is not in the capture. The check reads line by line and does not understand sentences, so a true number of the right signal used for the wrong thing would still pass; the answers are written from the capture's facts by a template, which never does that.
details.title: The answer check refuses a made-up number

details.text: The resolver, planner, build reuse, capture driver, answer writer and answer check are ordinary deterministic Python. They were written by an AI coding assistant to the owner's brief and checked by independent reviewers and the tests. At run time the only model call is reading the request, by openai/gpt-6-luna through a provider; nothing it says is trusted until the resolver has traced it in the RTL.
details.title: Who wrote what

details.text: Cycle 0 is the sample in which the trigger condition holds: there win_wr = 1 and addr = 0x80. The counter still shows 0x0003 in that sample and 0x1234 one clock later, because the register loads on the clock edge that ends the write strobe.
details.title: Where the trigger is, and why the counter changes one clock later

details.text: Not measured: there is no timed comparison with a person setting up the analyser by hand. Qualitatively, the request replaces choosing post-synthesis register names, packing ports within the free tier's limits, writing per-bit trigger values and reading the waveform; the build itself takes the same Vivado time either way, and a request served by an existing build needs no build at all.
details.title: What this saves, honestly

story.how: A language model only restates the request as structured JSON. Everything after it is deterministic: each signal name is resolved against the RTL (the design's source code) to a register output, the trigger becomes per-bit compare values, the window and the analyser's ports are sized within the free tier's limits, and the plan is shown before anything is built. The build reuses the normal Vivado flow and all its checks and is programmed into the board's volatile memory (SRAM, never the flash). The capture runs over the board's programming cable (JTAG) while the design is driven over its serial link; the answer is written from facts computed from the samples, and a check refuses any number that the capture does not support.
story.problem: An on-chip logic analyser (ILA: logic added to the design that records chosen signals into on-chip memory, one sample per clock) shows what a design really does on the board, but setting one up is slow: choosing signals that survive synthesis, packing them into the analyser's ports, writing the trigger, rebuilding and reading the waveform. On the free Basic licence tier of Vivado the analyser is also limited: one analyser per design, so one clock; at most 5 probe ports (groups of wires into the analyser); and one comparator per port (the hardware that tests a port against the trigger value). A request that does not fit fails late, after a long build.
results: 5 of 5 known-answer requests on one design passed: the answer matched the known result each time, and the value read back over the serial link in the 3 runs that read a register back. One run each, so no spread is stated. All five are in the table below.

5 debug builds of 418.1 to 531.8 seconds each (about 7 to 9 minutes): 4 served the requests and 1 was the OR layout that Vivado refused to arm, rebuilt with one port per OR term. 1 of the 5 requests needed no new build because an earlier build already held its signals. Every build met timing (worst setup slack at least 3.06 ns), at most 0.162 W estimated by Vivado.
Programming and capture took 48.3 to 64.7 seconds per request. Reading each request cost $0.00011 to $0.00027 per request, as the model provider reported.
All 5 captures ran inside the recommended operating conditions: die 24.7 to 26.9 C at the readings (latched maximum 27.68 C), core supply 1.006 V, 0 alarms.

projects.headline: A hardware checker that watches an AXI bus and names the rule a bug breaks. On the Digilent Nexys A7-100T (xc7a100tcsg324-1, Vivado 2026.1) it flagged the expected rule in all 6 runs with a seeded protocol bug (8 faults), and against our own peripheral and stream FIFO the board's traffic matched simulation cycle for cycle in 13 of 13 runs.

hero.caption: One capture from the board, one seeded bug: our peripheral raises the write-response valid signal (BVALID) before any write data has arrived, and the checker flags it in that cycle.

data.alt: A waveform captured on the board: after the address handshake the peripheral raises BVALID, its write response, before any write data; the checker's B_EARLY rule goes high in that cycle and the write data arrives afterwards.

projects.one_line: A block that sits on the chip beside the design under test, drives AXI4-Lite and AXI4-Stream traffic from a program loaded at run time, and checks a set of named protocol rules in hardware while the traffic runs.

approvals: The owner authorised hardware use (volatile configuration only, wall power)
Independent reviewers checked the work, and the owner merges it
gates: Every rule checked quiet and firing, every broken copy of the checker caught
Simulation of every program, seeded bug and memory fault
Vivado 2026.1 gates: methodology, timing, design rule checks, power
The board plan written in advance, with die temperature and rails logged
agent.plan: The owner chose the project and set the rules. A language-model coding agent wrote the RTL, the rule monitors (from the specification, in its own words), the seeded bugs, the proofs, the simulation and the board runs. The bugs were seeded by the same agent that wrote the checker; AMD's checker is the part it did not write.
agent.request: The owner asked for an on-chip AMBA AXI traffic generator and protocol checker that exercises on-chip modules with transactions of any complexity while verifying protocol correctness.

details.text: Checked on AXI4-Lite: AW_HOLD, W_HOLD, B_HOLD, AR_HOLD and R_HOLD (VALID held, payload stable, until READY); B_EARLY and R_EARLY (a response only after its request); RESET and IN_RESET (every VALID low at and during reset); EXOKAY (no exclusive-access response on AXI4-Lite). Checked on AXI4-Stream: HOLD, KEEP_STRB (a reserved byte marking) and RESET; two profile rules (a maximum packet length, packed bytes) are off unless an IP core documents them. Not checked: bursts, IDs, wrapping bursts, the four-kilobyte boundary and exclusive access, which belong to full AXI4; a combinational path from READY to VALID inside a block, of which only its effect at the ports shows; and data correctness, which the reference memory and the stream receiver check instead. False alarms matter as much as misses: each rule is proved quiet on all legal traffic within 20 cycles; in simulation, 11 scenarios of legal but unusual traffic (W before AW, a response in the same cycle as the next request, READY before VALID, a reset in mid-transaction, null and position stream bytes, non-contiguous byte-keeps) fired 0 rules; and the 9 clean board runs fired none.
details.title: Rules checked and not checked

story.how:
A transaction program, written in plain YAML and loaded over the serial link, drives AXI4-Lite traffic (a simple register-access bus) and AXI4-Stream traffic (a packet stream) with seeded random addresses, data and byte-enables (which bytes of a word to write), pauses by the sender and refusals by the receiver (back-pressure).

Monitors that watch only the bus wires check 10 AXI4-Lite and 5 AXI4-Stream rules every cycle. A reference copy of the memory checks reads of every word written in the run, counters record latency, stalls and which cases were covered, and the first violation starts a capture. The same program runs on the board and in simulation.
story.problem:
AXI is the on-chip bus defined by the AMBA specification IHI 0022H (its stream variant: IHI 0051B). A bus interface that breaks its handshake rules often passes a quick test and fails in a system: read data that is not held while the master stalls, or a write response sent before the data. Such bugs show only under the right timing, and a logic analyser shows the waveform but not which rule it breaks.

The hard part is the checker, not the traffic. A wrong checker passes bad designs or flags good ones, so this one is checked formally, attacked with deliberately broken copies of itself, and compared on the board with AMD's own checker.

The other hard part is making the board and the simulation see identical traffic: every random choice has to be seeded, and every counter has to start with the run.
results: 17 of 17 board runs, written in a plan before the board was used, gave the verdict the plan expected. The table says what each kind of run was checked against.
In one run against the board's block-RAM controller IP core, under random back-pressure, write latency ran from 2 to 12 cycles and read latency from 1 to 8.

Design size and timing: the whole board design used 7043 LUTs and met timing with 0.169 ns of slack; Vivado estimated 0.185 W. Measured on the die: at most 26.45 C, core supply (VCCINT) 1.0042 to 1.0078 V, inside the recommended operating conditions, 0 alarms latched.

Earlier attempts: the first, on an earlier build, passed 15 of 17; the transaction model and the RTL were then fixed and the whole plan run again on the final build (evidence: earlier board attempts).

The board runs need the board and are recorded in the evidence above.
